p: East Karelia, also called Eastern or Russian Karelia, is the part of Karelia beyond the eastern border of Finland which, since the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, has remained Eastern Orthodox and a part of Russia. It is distinguished from the western part, Finnish Karelia, which before 1808 was Swedish Karelia. It consists mainly of two old historical regions, Viena or White Karelia and Aunus or Olonets Karelia.

The Fennomans, ethnic nationalists of the 19th century, saw East Karelia as the ancient home of Finnic culture, untouched by Scandinavians or Slavs. In its sparsely populated backwoods, mainly in White Karelia, Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) collected the folk tales that became the Kalevala, published from 1835 to 1849. The idea of joining the region to a Greater Finland had wide support in newly independent Finland after 1917.

When Finland and Soviet Russia divided Karelia between them in 1920, the Soviet authorities promised far-reaching cultural rights to the Finnic peoples who made up most of East Karelia's population. Within the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic these rights were never realised, and under Stalin ethnic Finns were persecuted and an intensive programme of Russification began.

Annexation was most popular during the Continuation War of 1941–1944, when an expected German conquest of the Soviet Union made it seem feasible. Finnish forces occupied most of East Karelia from 1941 to 1944, and the war brought hardship to the local ethnic Russian civilians, including forced labour and internment in prison camps as enemy aliens. After the Moscow Armistice of September 1944 calls for annexation virtually disappeared.

Most of East Karelia is now part of the Republic of Karelia within the Russian Federation. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Finnic culture in the region has experienced a revival. In Finnish the region is called Itä-Karjala or Venäjän Karjala, and in Karelian Idä-Karjala.
